extracted.intended_audience: authors, editors, proofreaders, printers, and publishers working on formal publications
extracted.subtask_description: A publisher's style manual prescribing typographical, spelling, punctuation, capitalization, and compositional rules for preparing texts for print, with specimens and instructions for proofreaders and compositors.

rubrics_metrics.name: Application and flexibility of the rules
rubrics_metrics.description: Regulations are meant for the average case and must be applied with a certain degree of elasticity; exceptions will constantly occur and room is left for individual initiative and discretion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: No regulation is absolutely inviolable; deviations may be made where the peculiar nature of the subject-matter, emphasis, author preference, or typographical contingency suggests it. Each such case must be decided on its own merits; generally defer to the author's expressed wishes where no question of taste or logic is involved.

rubrics_metrics.name: 1. Proper nouns and adjectives
rubrics_metrics.description: CAPITALIZE— Proper nouns and adjectives: George, America, North America, Englishman; Elizabethan, French.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not capitalize verbs derived from proper names with specialized meaning (to boycott, to pasteurize), nor such words when used in special scientific or trade significance (volt, ampere, angstrom, etc.).

rubrics_metrics.name: 2. Epithets used as substitutes for proper names
rubrics_metrics.description: CAPITALIZE— Epithets used as substitutes for proper names, or affixed to a name: the Pretender, Bloody Mary, Richard the Lion-hearted, Alexander the Great.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples illustrate capitalization when epithet functions as part of the name.

rubrics_metrics.name: 3. Particles in French names
rubrics_metrics.description: CAPITALIZE— The particles in French names, as 'le,' 'la,' 'de,' 'du,' when they are not preceded by a Christian name or title; but do not capitalize them when preceded by such name or title.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: Le Bossu, La Torre, La Rochelle, De Coligny; but Rene le Bossu, Miguel de la Torre, Thomas d'Aubigne. Also notes on treatment of Dutch 'Van' (capitalize) and German 'von' (do not capitalize unless beginning a sentence), with listed exceptions (Henry van Dyke, J. H. van't Hoff).

rubrics_metrics.name: 4. Generic geographic terms forming part of names
rubrics_metrics.description: CAPITALIZE— Generic terms forming a part of geographical names: Atlantic Ocean, Dead Sea, Gulf of Mexico, Rocky Mountains, Mississippi River, etc.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not capitalize such words when merely added by way of description (the river Elbe, the desert of Sahara, the island of Madagascar). The manual provides lists of generic place-terms that are capitalized in singular or plural forms and positional rules (immediately following the name, before/after the name, etc.).

rubrics_metrics.name: 5. Adjectives and nouns distinguishing definite regions
rubrics_metrics.description: CAPITALIZE— Adjectives and nouns used singly or in conjunction to distinguish definite regions when used with a recognized geographical term: Old World, Western Hemisphere, Continental Europe, North Pole, the North, the East, the Middle West (United States).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not as a rule capitalize adjectives derived from such names when indicating direction: oriental customs, the southern states, a southerner (but Northman = Scandinavian). For world-wide application capitalize (Eastern peoples; Western nations).

rubrics_metrics.name: 6. Generic terms for political divisions
rubrics_metrics.description: CAPITALIZE— When the term is an organic part of the name (German Empire, United Kingdom); when used with 'of' as integral part indicating certain subdivisions (Department of the Lakes); when used singly as accepted designation (the Union, the States); when part of fanciful/popular appellations used as if real geographical names (Celestial Empire, Garden City).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not capitalize such terms when standing alone or used generically (the empire, the state; empire of Russia, kingdom of Servia).

rubrics_metrics.name: 7. Numbered political divisions
rubrics_metrics.description: CAPITALIZE— Numbered political divisions used as names: Eleventh Congressional District, First Ward, Second Precinct.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: References to rule 100 for additional numbering rules.

rubrics_metrics.name: 8. Names of thoroughfares, parks, squares, blocks, buildings
rubrics_metrics.description: CAPITALIZE— Specific names of streets, parks, squares, blocks, buildings: Drexel Avenue, Lincoln Park, Trafalgar Square, Monadnock Block, Lakeside Building, Capitol, White House.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not capitalize general designations such as 'courthouse,' 'post-office,' 'library' except when forming part of a proper name tied to a place.

rubrics_metrics.name: 9. Names of parties, denominations, schools and their adherents
rubrics_metrics.description: CAPITALIZE— Names of political parties, religious denominations or sects, philosophical, literary, and artistic schools, and their adherents: Republican, Catholic, Evangelical Lutheran, the Romantic movement, Symbolic school of painters.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not capitalize these words or their derivatives when used in a general or acquired sense (republican form of government, socialism as an economic panacea, evangelical spirit).

rubrics_metrics.name: 10. Names of monastic orders and their members
rubrics_metrics.description: CAPITALIZE— Names of monastic orders and their members: Black Friars, Dominican, Jesuit.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Straightforward capitalization when referring to specific orders/members.

rubrics_metrics.name: 11. Proper (official) titles of organizations and institutions
rubrics_metrics.description: CAPITALIZE— Official titles of social, religious, educational, political, commercial, and industrial organizations and institutions: Union League Club, Smithsonian Institution, State University of Iowa, The Macmillan Company.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not capitalize such generic terms when used to designate a class or standing alone (the club, the association) unless to avoid ambiguity or in rare conventional uses (He joined the Hall [Tammany]).

rubrics_metrics.name: 12. Legislative, judiciary, administrative bodies and departments
rubrics_metrics.description: CAPITALIZE— Names of legislative, judiciary, and administrative bodies and departments when specifically applied: Congress, Parliament, Supreme Court of the United States, Department of the Interior.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not capitalize general or paraphrastic designations (the national assembly, the legislature of the state, the council).

rubrics_metrics.name: 13. Ordinals for dynasties, sessions, regiments
rubrics_metrics.description: CAPITALIZE— Ordinals used to designate Egyptian dynasties, sessions of Congress, names of regiments: the Eighteenth Dynasty, the Fifty-third Congress, the Second Illinois Regiment Band.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: But do not capitalize common dynastic words (the Ming dynasty). See rule 100 for numbering.

rubrics_metrics.name: 14. Historical epochs, language/literary periods, geological ages
rubrics_metrics.description: CAPITALIZE— Commonly accepted appellations for historical epochs, periods in the history of a language or literature, geological ages/strata: Crusades, Renaissance, Reformation, Neolithic age (but: Stone Age, Middle Ages).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not capitalize informal adjectives in such phrases (early Algonkian, late Permian). Capitalize 'Age' only where failure to do so would be ambiguous.

rubrics_metrics.name: 15. Names of important events
rubrics_metrics.description: CAPITALIZE— Names of important historical events: Thirty Years' War, Peasants' War, Revolutionary War, Battle of Gettysburg, Louisiana Purchase.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat as proper names of events; follow examples.

rubrics_metrics.name: 16. Political alliances and historically significant terms
rubrics_metrics.description: CAPITALIZE— Political alliances and terms that have acquired special significance as party or movement names: Protestant League, Holy Alliance, the Roses, Independents.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: See rule 9 for related treatment.

rubrics_metrics.name: 17. Conventions, congresses, expositions
rubrics_metrics.description: CAPITALIZE— Names of conventions, congresses, expositions: Council of Nicaea, Parliament of Religions, Westminster Assembly, Chicago World's Fair.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Capitalize full, specific titles of assembled events.

rubrics_metrics.name: 18. Titles of treaties, acts, laws, bills
rubrics_metrics.description: CAPITALIZE— Titles of specific treaties, acts, laws, and bills: Treaty of Verdun, Article V of the Peace of Prague, Declaration of Independence, Magna Carta, Fourteenth Amendment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Capitalize the specific title of the juridical document when used as a proper name.

rubrics_metrics.name: 19. Creeds and confessions of faith
rubrics_metrics.description: CAPITALIZE— Creeds and confessions: Apostles' Creed, Nicene Creed, Augsburg Confession, Thirty-nine Articles.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use capitalization for historically recognized creeds; note exceptions for antecedent or adjectival forms (ante-Nicene).

rubrics_metrics.name: 20. Civic holidays and ecclesiastical fast and feast days
rubrics_metrics.description: CAPITALIZE— Civic holidays and ecclesiastical observances: Fourth of July (the Fourth), Labor Day, Thanksgiving Day; Easter, Passover, Feast of Tabernacles.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat these as formal names of days/holidays.

rubrics_metrics.name: 21. Titles of honor and respect and academic degrees
rubrics_metrics.description: CAPITALIZE— Titles of honor/respect (religious, civil, military) preceding the name and academic degrees following the name; all titles of honor or nobility referring to specific persons: Queen Victoria, Rear-Admiral Dewey, Doctor of Philosophy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not capitalize the official title when it follows the name (Woodrow Wilson, president of the United States) or when standing alone without referring to the existing incumbent; numerous examples and exceptions provided (see rule 49 and related notes).

rubrics_metrics.name: 22. Abbreviations like Ph.D., M.P., and celestial designations
rubrics_metrics.description: CAPITALIZE— Abbreviations like Ph.D., M.P., F.R.G.S. and designations of celestial objects; set without spaces between letters.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Set such abbreviated titles without spaces between letters; see cross-references to other rules (52, 103, 106).

rubrics_metrics.name: 23. One-letter abbreviations
rubrics_metrics.description: CAPITALIZE— Abbreviations consisting of one letter except for units of measurement and minor literary subdivisions: R.V. (Revised Version), C. (centigrade), A (angstrom units) — but not p., l., n., etc.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use capitals for one-letter abbreviations representative of significant named items.

rubrics_metrics.name: 24. Nouns and adjectives designating the Supreme Being
rubrics_metrics.description: CAPITALIZE— Nouns and adjectives designating the Supreme Being or any member of the Christian Trinity, and pronouns referring to the same, when not closely preceded or followed by a distinctive name: the Almighty, Father, Son, Holy Ghost, Savior, Messiah.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not capitalize derived expressions (God's fatherhood, messianic) in ordinary contexts; exceptions exist when personification or emphasis justifies capitalization.

rubrics_metrics.name: 25. Words with acquired, limited, or special meaning
rubrics_metrics.description: CAPITALIZE— Words that have an acquired, limited, or special meaning: the Doctor's degree; a Bachelor's hood; a Freshman.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not capitalize the generic forms (the doctorate, a master in chancery) when capitalization no longer indicates special meaning.

rubrics_metrics.name: 26. Personified abstract ideas
rubrics_metrics.description: CAPITALIZE— 'Nature' and similar terms, and abstract ideas, when personified: 'Nature wields her scepter...' 'Vice in the old English morality plays.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Capitalize when a concept is personified; otherwise use lower case.

rubrics_metrics.name: 27. 'Father' and 'Reformers' in ambiguous contexts
rubrics_metrics.description: CAPITALIZE— 'Father' used for church father and 'Reformers' used of Reformation leaders whenever meaning would otherwise be ambiguous: the Fathers, the Reformers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use capitalization to avoid ambiguity; otherwise lower-case explanatory usages (the church reformers of the fifteenth century).

rubrics_metrics.name: 28. 'Church' in properly cited titles
rubrics_metrics.description: CAPITALIZE— The word 'church' in properly cited titles of nationally organized bodies or when forming part of the name of a particular edifice: Church of Rome, Church of England, Fifth Avenue Baptist Church.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not capitalize 'church' when standing alone (the church = organized Christianity) unless exceptional rhetorical emphasis is intended.

rubrics_metrics.name: 29. Names for the Bible and other sacred books
rubrics_metrics.description: CAPITALIZE— Names for the Bible and other sacred books: Scriptures, Holy Writ, Book of Books; Koran, Vedas, Mishna, Upanishads.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not capitalize adjectives derived from such nouns (biblical, scriptural, koranic, vedic).

rubrics_metrics.name: 30. Versions and editions of the Bible
rubrics_metrics.description: CAPITALIZE— Versions and editions of the Bible: King James's Version, Authorized Version (A.V.), Revised Version (R.V.), Septuagint (LXX).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use capitalization for commonly cited named versions; see abbreviations guidance.

rubrics_metrics.name: 31. Books and divisions of sacred works
rubrics_metrics.description: CAPITALIZE— Books and divisions of the Bible and other sacred books: Old Testament, Pentateuch, Exodus, Second Kings, Psalms, Gospel of Luke, Acts of the Apostles, Epistle to the Romans.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not capitalize common nouns like 'book,' 'gospel,' 'epistle,' 'psalm' in contexts such as 'the five books of Moses' or 'the first forty psalms.'

rubrics_metrics.name: 32. Biblical parables
rubrics_metrics.description: CAPITALIZE— Names of biblical parables when referenced as titles: the parable of the Prodigal Son.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat the parable title as a proper name.

rubrics_metrics.name: 33. Miscellaneous biblical terms
rubrics_metrics.description: CAPITALIZE— Miscellaneous terms with special biblical significance: Last Supper, Eucharist, the Passion, the Twelve (apostles), the Golden Rule, the Kingdom of God.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Capitalize standardized religious terms of reference.

rubrics_metrics.name: 34. First word of a sentence and poetry lines
rubrics_metrics.description: CAPITALIZE— The first word of a sentence, and in poetry the first word of each line.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Exception: In Greek and Latin poetry capitalize only the first word of a paragraph, not each verse (examples provided).

rubrics_metrics.name: 35. First word after a colon
rubrics_metrics.description: CAPITALIZE— The first word after a colon only when introducing a complete passage or sentence with independent meaning, as in summarizations and quotations not closely connected with what precedes; or where the colon has the weight of 'as follows,' 'namely.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not capitalize if the quotation is immediately connected with preceding clause or if the colon introduces a brief explanatory phrase or a note of comment. Examples: 'In conclusion I wish to say: It will be seen...' vs 'The old adage is true that "haste makes waste".'

rubrics_metrics.name: 36. First word in sections of an enumeration
rubrics_metrics.description: CAPITALIZE— As a rule, the first word in sections of an enumeration when any one link contains two or more distinct clauses separated by semicolon, colon, or period, unless all are dependent on the same leading term.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples illustrate when each enumerated item begins with a capitalized first word versus lower-case when all dependent (see examples in text).

rubrics_metrics.name: 37. Nouns followed by numerals (sequence indicators)
rubrics_metrics.description: CAPITALIZE— Nouns followed by a numeral indicating order in a sequence: Room 16, Ps. 20, Grade IV, Act I, Vol. I, No. 2, Book II.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not capitalize minor subdivisions of publications such as 'sec. 4,' 'scene i,' 'art. iii' (see 'no.').

rubrics_metrics.name: 38. First word of cited speech in direct discourse
rubrics_metrics.description: CAPITALIZE— The first word of a cited speech (or thought) in direct discourse, whether preceded by a colon or comma.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: On leaving he remarked: 'Never shall I forget this day'; With the words, 'Never shall I forget this day,' he departed; or without quotation marks: I thought to myself: This day I shall never forget.

rubrics_metrics.name: 39. First words following 'WHEREAS' and 'Resolved'
rubrics_metrics.description: CAPITALIZE— In resolutions, the first words following 'WHEREAS' and 'Resolved' are capitalized: WHEREAS, It has pleased God...; Resolved, That ...
rubrics_metrics.guidance: See rule 51 for use of caps and small caps in resolutions.

rubrics_metrics.name: 40. Exclamations 'O' and 'Oh'
rubrics_metrics.description: CAPITALIZE— The exclamations 'O' and 'Oh' should be capitalized in direct address/exclamation: 'O Lord!' 'Oh, that I were home again!'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat vocatives and exclamatory interjections as sentence-initial words when appropriate.

rubrics_metrics.name: 41. Capitalization of principal words in English titles
rubrics_metrics.description: CAPITALIZE— All the principal words (nouns, pronouns, adjectives, adverbs, verbs, first and last words) in English titles of publications and their divisions; also in subjects of lectures, cap-and-small-cap and italic center-heads, bold-face cut-in heads and side-heads, and cap-and-small-cap box-heads in tables.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: The Men Who Made the Nation; note exceptions e.g., Botanical Gazette practice of capitalizing only first words and proper names in bibliographies; side-heads should avoid full capitalization (see rule 56 and 172).

rubrics_metrics.name: 42. Capitalization in foreign titles
rubrics_metrics.description: CAPITALIZE— In foreign titles, capitalize the first word and follow language-specific rules: Latin — capitalize proper nouns and derived adjectives; French/Italian/Spanish/Swedish/Norwegian — capitalize proper nouns but not derived adjectives; German/Danish — capitalize all nouns but not adjectives; Dutch — capitalize all nouns and adjectives derived from proper nouns.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples provided: De amicitia; Histoire de la litterature frangaise; Geschichte des deutschen Feudalwesens; Geschiedenis der Nederlandsche Taal.

rubrics_metrics.name: 43. Treatment of definite article in newspaper/magazine titles
rubrics_metrics.description: CAPITALIZE— In mentioning titles of newspapers, magazines, and similar publications do not, as a rule, treat the definite article as part of the title: the Chicago Tribune, the School Review.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Omit 'The' as part of the title in running text except where specifically part of the title in citations.

rubrics_metrics.name: 44. Titles of ancient manuscripts
rubrics_metrics.description: CAPITALIZE— Titles of ancient manuscripts (singular MS; plural MSS): Codex Bernensis, Cod. Canonicianus.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat manuscript titles as proper names, apply abbreviation conventions.

rubrics_metrics.name: 45. Capitalization in hyphenated titles
rubrics_metrics.description: CAPITALIZE— In titles with main words capitalized, capitalize all nouns forming parts of hyphenated compounds (Twentieth-Century Progress; The Economy of High-Speed Trains).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not capitalize hyphenated components when they are not nouns (Fifty-first Street, 'World-Dominion of English-speaking Peoples'). Side-head rules differ (capitalize only first word and proper nouns).

rubrics_metrics.name: 46. Scientific (Latin) names in biological/geological contexts
rubrics_metrics.description: CAPITALIZE— In botanical, geological, zoological, and paleontological matter, capitalize scientific (Latin) names of divisions, orders, families, and genera but not their English derivatives: Cotylosauria (but cotylosaurs); Felidae (but felids).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Names of species derived from persons or generic names may be capitalized in botanical/zoological usage; in geological and medical contexts species names are never capitalized. Examples: Felis leo, Cocos nucifera, Rosa Carolina (but geological example Pterygomatopus schmidti). See rule 71 for italics treatment.

rubrics_metrics.name: 47. Names and epithets of peoples, races, tribes
rubrics_metrics.description: CAPITALIZE— Names and epithets of peoples, races, and tribes: Kafir, Negro (in ethnic sense), Hottentot, Makassar, Buginese, Celestials.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use capitalization for ethnic/national/tribal names; indexing and usage notes may apply (see index references).

rubrics_metrics.name: 48. Astronomical names and catalogue designations
rubrics_metrics.description: CAPITALIZE— In astronomical work, capitalize names of planetary bodies, stars, and groups of stars (Saturn, Ursa Major, Milky Way, Great Bear); designations of celestial objects in well-known catalogues and Flamsteed numbers (M 13, N.G.C. 6165, 85 Pegasi).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not capitalize generic 'sun,' 'earth,' 'moon,' 'stars' in ordinary contexts unless in astronomical works where names may be treated specially (see cross-reference).

rubrics_metrics.name: 49. University-specific divisions and titles (University of Chicago)
rubrics_metrics.description: CAPITALIZE— Divisions, departments, officers, and courses of study of the University of Chicago in all official work dealing with its administration or curricula: the School of Education, the Department of Anthropology, the Board of Trustees, the President, Professor of Physics.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When used in official contexts these institutional names and titles are capitalized; ordinary references in non-official contexts may use lower case (the division, the scholarship).

rubrics_metrics.name: 50. Use of caps and small capitals for date lines and salutations
rubrics_metrics.description: USE CAPITALS AND SMALL CAPITALS FOR— The names of town and state in the date line, and the salutatory phrase at the beginning of letters, and the signature and residence at the end of letters or articles: CHICAGO, ILL., January 1, 1911; MY DEAR MR. SMITH:; CHARLES W. SCOTT.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Set to the right/left with specified indentation and in smaller type; each line of address in caps and small caps, centered; explanatory typesetting guidance provided.

rubrics_metrics.name: 51. Use of small caps for SECTION/NOTE and WHEREAS
rubrics_metrics.description: USE CAPITALS AND SMALL CAPITALS FOR— In resolutions, the word 'WHEREAS'; in notes (not footnotes), the word 'NOTE' (followed by a period and dash); in constitutions/by-laws the word 'SECTION' introducing paragraphs and followed by a number.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Usual practice is to abbreviate 'section' after first occurrence: SECTION 1. ... SEC. 2. ...; 'NOTE. — It should be noticed that...'.

rubrics_metrics.name: 52. Set A.M., P.M., B.C., A.D. in small capitals without spaces
rubrics_metrics.description: SET IN SMALL CAPITALS— A.M. and P.M. (ante and post meridiem), and B.C. and A.D. should be set without a space between the letters: 11:30 A.M.; 53 B.C., 1906 A.D.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cross-references to rules on abbreviation spacing (see 22, 103, 106, 219).

rubrics_metrics.name: 53. Use lower-case initial for commonized former proper names and derivatives
rubrics_metrics.description: USE SMALL (i.e., 'lower-case') INITIAL LETTER FOR— Words of common usage originally proper names, and their derivatives in whose present generalized acceptation the origin has become obscured; generally all verbs derived from proper names: Utopia, bohemian, philistine, titanic, platonic, quixotic, bonan...
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Verbs and terms that have become common nouns/adjectives or verbs from proper names (to boycott, to posterize) should be lower-case; rule continues with examples and cross-references.
